article.audioclf.title: Fine-tuning DistilHuBERT for music genre classification
article.audioclf.subtitle: Deep learning audio project based on the GTZAN dataset: audio signal preprocessing, adaptation of a pretrained transformer, and performance analysis on a classification task.
article.audioclf.overview.title: Goal
article.audioclf.overview.text: The goal here was to automatically classify music excerpts by genre directly from raw audio signals. The project shows how to prepare waveforms, convert them into the format expected by DistilHuBERT, and fine-tune the model to recognize 10 different music genres.
article.audioclf.dataset.title: Data
article.audioclf.dataset.text: The project uses GTZAN, a classic music classification dataset composed of 1000 audio excerpts distributed across 10 genres. Each track corresponds to a 30-second excerpt. Since the dataset is relatively balanced, a simple train/test split is enough to evaluate the model’s behavior on unseen data.
article.audioclf.preprocessing.title: Audio preprocessing
article.audioclf.preprocessing.text: The excerpts are resampled to 16 kHz to match the format expected by the pretrained model. Preprocessing is applied on the fly (inside the training loop) through the feature extractor. It resizes the inputs if needed, normalizes them, and converts them into tensors usable by the transformer. This approach avoids storing all precomputed data at once and keeps the pipeline lighter.
article.audioclf.model.title: Model
article.audioclf.model.text:
The model used is DistilHuBERT, a distilled and lighter version of HuBERT with around 23 million parameters. Unlike models working on spectrograms, DistilHuBERT directly takes a raw, resampled, and normalized waveform as input.

I chose it because it is more compact than large audio transformers while still keeping representations learned from massive amounts of audio data. It is therefore a good compromise for a fine-tuning notebook: powerful enough to obtain strong results while remaining easier to train on Google Colab.

Concretely, the fine-tuning process reuses the pretrained model, which already knows how to extract general audio representations, and replaces the classification head with one adapted to GTZAN’s 10 genres. Training then adjusts the model weights to specialize these representations on my music dataset instead of learning the whole audio structure from scratch.
article.audioclf.training.title: Training
article.audioclf.training.text: Training is performed using the Hugging Face Trainer. The notebook defines the main hyperparameters: batch size, gradient accumulation, learning rate, scheduler, warmup, weight decay, and evaluation at each epoch. After a first training phase, a second fine-tuning stage is launched with a different learning rate to improve validation accuracy.
article.audioclf.inference.title: Evaluation
article.audioclf.inference.text: After training, the model is evaluated on the test set. The analysis does not stop at overall accuracy: a confusion matrix and a classification report help identify which genres are well separated and which ones remain harder to distinguish.
article.audioclf.results.title: Results
article.audioclf.results.text: The notebook reaches a test accuracy of around 87%, which is a strong result on GTZAN for a relatively small model. Most genres are recognized correctly. The main confusions mostly happen between rock, metal, and country, which makes sense since these styles share many instrumental characteristics such as guitar, bass, and drums. In this case, the confusion matrix helps show the relationship between the model’s errors and actual musical similarities.
article.audioclf.conclusion.title: Conclusion and future work
article.audioclf.conclusion.text:
This project allowed me to build a complete audio classification pipeline using a pretrained transformer. Fine-tuning DistilHuBERT makes it possible to obtain strong performance without training a model from scratch, by adapting general audio representations to a specific music classification task.

The results are very encouraging, with an accuracy close to 87%. The remaining errors mostly come from musically similar genres, showing that the limitation does not only come from the model itself but also from the nature of the classes. To go further, it would be interesting to test additional music genres or build a small inference interface to try the model on new tracks.
